AfriScan by Afridrone · Angola

Know what is built inside your pipeline or power-line strip in Angola

We locate the houses and other structures along oil and gas pipelines, transmission lines and railways, and map land change in mining concessions and project areas. Each structure is measured to the line and grouped by band, a person reviews every result, and you receive GIS files and a PDF report in English or Portuguese. Satellite first; drones only where a stretch needs the detail.

The law behind the register Lei n.º 9/04 (Lei de Terras) art. 27 · Decreto n.º 120/08 art. 11 · Código Mineiro (Lei n.º 31/11) arts. 200–207 · Lei n.º 1/21 art. 33 · Lei da Aviação Civil art. 16.º-A

The 30 m strip

What Angola’s Land Law says about land beside pipes and lines

Angola’s Land Law places a 30 m strip on each side of electricity, water, telecom, oil and gas installations and conductors among its partial reserves. Our register measures each structure against that strip and against the widths you add.

  • Lei n.º 9/04, de 9 de Novembro (Lei de Terras), art. 27(7)(g): partial reserves include “os terrenos ocupados por auto-estradas, por estradas de quatro faixas e por instalações e condutores de electricidade, água, telecomunicações, petróleo e gás com uma faixa confinante de 30m de cada lado” (land occupied by motorways, four-lane roads and electricity, water, telecom, oil and gas installations and conductors, with an adjoining strip of 30 m on each side).
  • What the strip allows (n.º 6): every form of occupation or use that does not collide with the purposes set in the reserve’s constituting instrument.
  • Land the State does not own (n.º 9–10): it enters a reserve only by expropriation for public utility or by administrative servitude, and fair compensation is always due.
  • Who creates reserves (n.º 2): the Government. Whether the 30 m strip binds a given stretch without its own constituting act is a question for the project’s counsel; the register shows what stands inside it either way.
  • Before petroleum operations: Decreto n.º 120/08 requires the area’s social and population structure and its land-rights holders to be assessed before a prospecting licence, and the assessment to be updated before exploration and again before development and production, including along pipeline routes and “servidões legais de passagem” (art. 11).

We measure the 30 m strip and the widths in your concession contract, a constituted servitude or your company standard. Each structure is recorded with its distance to the line, so the servitude team knows what sits inside each band and how close it is to the pipe or conductor.

As of 27 September 2026. A summary of published rules, with sources; it is not legal advice.

Why it matters

What builds up between two visits

A pipeline, a transmission line or a concession covers more ground than any team can walk. Occupation of a servitude rarely starts as a whole bairro: it starts with one house, then the one beside it.

Between patrols, houses and outbuildings go up beside the strip, fields (lavras) and tracks open, and someone digs or clears ground near the asset. By the time anyone notices, what could have been handled early has become a servitude negotiation, a line in a resettlement plan or an argument about who was there first.

In Angola the timing matters in law as well as on the ground. In expropriation by zones or alignments, compensation for property outside the first zone counts the necessary improvements (benfeitorias necessárias) made between the declaration of public utility and taking possession (Lei n.º 1/21, art. 33). A dated register on each of those dates separates what existed from what came later.

Structures inside each band

A register of the structures within the widths you choose, with the distance to the line or boundary, the coordinates and the segment of the route each one sits in.

Tracks, clearing and excavations

Change between dated surveys, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, so field teams know where to go.

What was there, and on which date

A register on a known date, such as a census cut-off date or a declaration of public utility, to support compensation, resettlement and dialogue with communities.

What you receive

A register your servitude, land and GIS teams can use at once

  • Counts by band and by 500 m segment, with the densest segments highlighted, so you know where to send teams first.
  • Each structure’s distance to the line, its band, its coordinates and a unique reference.
  • The source of every image and, where the source records it, the capture date.
  • A PDF report in English or Portuguese, with maps, the segment table, a view of each structure and the coordinate register.
  • GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile, and an interactive map file that opens in a browser, in the field too.

Resettlement and ESIA

Dated registers for cut-off dates, expropriation and regrouping

Cut-off dates. On lender-financed projects the lender applies standards such as IFC Performance Standard 5 or the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standard 5, and the census cut-off date decides who is eligible for compensation. A register made from dated imagery supports the cut-off-date record and shows what appeared afterwards. It does not replace the census, the asset inventory or consultation with the families concerned.

Expropriation by zones. Lei n.º 1/21 leaves forced removal and resettlement operations to their own instrument (art. 2(2)–(3)), and counts improvements made between the declaration of public utility and possession in the compensation for later zones (art. 33).

Mining zones and regrouping. The Mining Code bars residence in restricted zones and allows the zones to be created only if the residents are regrouped nearby, in housing “nunca inferiores” (never inferior) to what they had, with equivalent social infrastructure (Lei n.º 31/11, art. 207). A dated count of structures before and after is the kind of baseline such a programme starts from.

Environmental licensing. The impact-assessment procedure is set by Decreto Presidencial n.º 117/20. Our layers drop into the ESIA (EIAS) team’s maps.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. We do not identify, count or follow people or vehicles, and whether a structure is authorised is for you, the authorities and, where it comes to that, the courts to decide.

Reviewed by a person

Automatic detection and building databases propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What the imagery cannot settle is listed for ground checks.

Dated, credited sources

Every report states its sources and, where the source records it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never real-time

Satellites and drones capture on particular dates, and rainy-season cloud delays optical imagery. Re-surveys follow the schedule agreed with you.

Supports your decisions

Dated registers support community dialogue, compensation processes and cut-off-date records. They do not replace your census, your surveyors or your engineers.

Satellite first, drones with ANAC authorisation

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite screening starts from the route file and dated imagery, open building databases or imagery you already hold. No aircraft flies and nobody needs to go on site, however long the strip. AfriScan is Afridrone’s land and corridor monitoring service; Afridrone flies the drone work.

Where satellite imagery is not enough, we propose drone surveys of the flagged stretches, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. In Angola, no aircraft able to fly without a pilot may overfly the territory without a special authorisation from the Autoridade Nacional da Aviação Civil (Lei da Aviação Civil, art. 16.º-A), and aerial photography, photogrammetry and aerial topography are specialised aerial services whose requirements ANAC sets (arts. 54–55).

Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals Angola requires. Every drone proposal says who flies, under which authorisations and on what timetable.

Who authorises what, in short

  • ANAC: the special authorisation for each flight, aerial-work licensing and aircraft registration (Lei n.º 28/21, art. 37; Lei da Aviação Civil, arts. 16.º-A and 156).
  • IGCA: alvarás for cartography, topography and GIS, and homologation of geographic information (Decreto Presidencial n.º 115/21, art. 6).
  • Mining-right holders and concessionaires: access to the restricted and protection zones of mines (Código Mineiro, arts. 200–203) and to line servitudes.
  • APD: processing and transfer of personal data (Lei n.º 22/11).

Drone law in Angola: the guide

Where we work

The scope of field and drone work

We do no field or drone work in Cabinda province outside Cabinda city, or in the provinces of Lunda Norte and Lunda Sul. That follows current travel advice: the UK advises against all but essential travel to Cabinda province except Cabinda city, and against travel to Lunda Norte and Lunda Sul unless absolutely necessary (FCDO, updated 28 May 2026); Canada advises avoiding non-essential travel to Cabinda and Lunda Norte (Travel Canada, 24 September 2026).

The same UK advice notes mines and unexploded weapons in many parts of the country. In the other provinces, any field work or flight therefore starts with an assessment of that risk agreed with the project, and keeps to the routes the project sets.

In short

  • Satellite screening from the route file, with no travel.
  • Drone and field work only with the approvals and security clearances each job requires and a safety plan agreed with the project.
  • No field or drone work in Cabinda outside the city, or in the Lundas.

For procurement and compliance teams

Tenders, local content and data

We answer tenders, requests for quotation and requests for proposal. Send the supplier-registration or prequalification forms with your request and tell us which portal or format your process uses. In the petroleum sector, Decreto Presidencial n.º 271/20 sets exclusivity, preference and competition regimes for suppliers; our guide to it is in Portuguese.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Angola?

The 30 m strip on each side that the Land Law attaches to electricity, water, telecom, oil and gas installations and conductors (Lei n.º 9/04, art. 27(7)(g)), and any width you give us, such as the one in your concession contract, a constituted servitude or a company standard, for example 60 m and 100 m. In a mining concession we measure the zones from the polygons you send. One survey can carry up to six widths.

Does a satellite-only survey need ANAC authorisation?

The Civil Aviation Law’s authorisations concern aircraft, and no aircraft flies in satellite work. That is a reading of the text, not legal advice. If the deliverables are meant as official cartography or geographic information, check with IGCA whether an alvará or homologation applies (Decreto Presidencial n.º 115/21, art. 6). See drone law in Angola.

Can the report be in Portuguese?

Yes. The PDF report comes in Portuguese or English, so the same register can go to the land team in Luanda, a provincial government and an international lender. The GIS layers open in QGIS, ArcGIS and Google Earth.

Do you work in every province?

We do no field or drone work in Cabinda province outside Cabinda city, or in Lunda Norte and Lunda Sul, in line with current travel advice. Elsewhere, any field or drone work starts with a landmine and unexploded-ordnance risk assessment agreed with the project.

Is the register a topographic or cadastral survey?

No. It is an inventory of structures and land change made from imagery, for managing servitudes and concessions. Official cartography and the property cadastre belong to IGCA, which grants the alvarás for that work and homologates geographic information (Decreto Presidencial n.º 115/21, art. 6).

Does the register hold personal data?

It describes structures and land, with no names, ID numbers or photographs of people. Household lists, where a project keeps them, stay with you. Lei n.º 22/11 makes processing personal data subject to prior notification to the data-protection agency (APD) or its authorisation (art. 35), and a transfer to a country without adequate protection always needs APD authorisation (art. 34).

Will you publish our route or results?

No. We never publish a client’s route, imagery or results without written permission. The sample on this site, a high-pressure gas pipeline in Mozambique, is shown with the route owner’s permission.

Know what stands inside the strip before the next servitude negotiation.

Send the route or site boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the province and the widths that matter: 30 m, your concession's, or the zones of a mining right. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
